title: Night Owls Are Not Just Tired. A New Study Says They Are Lonelier, and It Is Making Them Anxious.
excerpt: Research presented at SLEEP 2026 finds that nocturnal loneliness is the key pathway linking late sleep patterns to higher anxiety — a finding that hits close to home for South Asians staying up to call family across time zones.
body:
If you are someone who naturally gravitates toward late nights — working after the household quiets down, scrolling through your phone at 1 AM, or staying up for a call with parents in Mumbai or Chennai — a new study suggests the problem is not just the lost sleep. It is what happens to your mind while you are awake and everyone else is asleep.

Research to be presented at the SLEEP 2026 annual meeting by scientists at Brigham Young University found that people with evening chronotypes — those who prefer going to bed and waking up later — report significantly higher levels of anxiety. But the study's most striking finding is about *why*. The answer is not simply disrupted circadian rhythms or blue-light exposure. It is loneliness. Specifically, nocturnal loneliness.

## The Loneliness No One Talks About

The researchers examined both daytime and nighttime social experiences of participants and found that evening chronotypes experienced greater loneliness overall, but the nighttime variety was especially potent. When they statistically accounted for nocturnal loneliness, the direct link between being a night owl and being anxious disappeared. In other words, it was not the late bedtime itself driving anxiety — it was the isolation that came with it.

"People with later sleep patterns reported poorer mental health in part because they also experienced greater loneliness, including feelings of loneliness at night, and increased levels of anxiety," said Alec Harlow, the study's lead author at Brigham Young University.

The American Academy of Sleep Medicine defines healthy sleep as requiring adequate duration, good quality, appropriate timing and regularity, and the absence of sleep disturbances. Evening chronotypes often fail on at least two of those dimensions — timing and regularity — because their natural preferences clash with the schedules society imposes.

## Why This Matters for the Diaspora

For millions of South Asians living in the United States, late nights are not a lifestyle choice — they are a structural reality. The nine-and-a-half to thirteen-hour time difference between the U.S. and India means that if you want to catch your parents after dinner in Delhi, you are making that call at midnight in New York or 9 PM in San Francisco. Weekend family calls routinely stretch past 1 AM.

Then there is the work dimension. The tech industry, which employs a disproportionate share of Indian Americans, runs on late-night Slack messages, on-call rotations, and the pressure to be available across time zones. A 2024 Pew Research Center survey found that Indian Americans work some of the longest hours of any immigrant group in the country.

The combination — late work hours followed by family calls to India followed by the silence of an empty living room at 2 AM — is a textbook recipe for the kind of nocturnal loneliness this study describes. And unlike general loneliness, which can be addressed through more social contact during the day, nocturnal loneliness is harder to fix because it is inherently tied to a moment when most of your social world is offline.

## What Actually Helps

Sleep researchers increasingly recommend what they call "social chronotherapy" — restructuring not just when you sleep, but when you socialize. For night owls, that means finding ways to feel socially connected during the late hours rather than eliminating them entirely.

For South Asian families, this might mean shifting the family call to a slightly earlier window, even if it means catching parents during their morning tea instead of after dinner. It might mean joining online communities or group chats that are active at night. Or it might mean something as simple as watching a show with your partner or roommate instead of alone.

The study also found that general loneliness — the daytime variety — was a mediating factor as well. People who felt connected during the day were partially buffered against the anxiety effects of late-night isolation. Building stronger daytime social habits, from lunchtime walks with colleagues to weekend gatherings, can serve as an insurance policy against what happens when the lights go off.

## The Bigger Sleep Picture

This study arrives alongside several other SLEEP 2026 presentations painting a broader picture of how sleep shapes long-term health. A separate study from the University of South Florida found that sleep problems in midlife predict lower psychological well-being nine years later, with the effect being stronger in women than men. Another found that adults who feel older than their actual age report worse insomnia, worse sleep regularity, and more daytime impairment — even after controlling for depression and anxiety.

For South Asians — a population with elevated cardiovascular risk, higher rates of diabetes, and a cultural tendency to deprioritize sleep — these findings are not abstract. They are a direct warning. The late-night WhatsApp call may feel like connection, but if it is consistently pushing your bedtime past midnight and leaving you alone in a quiet apartment at 2 AM, it may be doing more harm than you realize.

The fix is not to stop calling home. It is to recognize that loneliness at night hits differently, and to build your evenings around people — not screens — whenever you can.
